excerpt: Trapped in the Philippines after Pearl Harbor, Chief Nurse Laura Cobb and ten Navy nurses endured thirty-seven months of captivity across Santo Tomas and Los Baños. Through starvation, disease, and relentless camp hardships, they improvised hospitals and saved lives—entering history as the Navy's resilient Band of Eleven.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
With two decades of service behind her, Chief Nurse Laura Cobb was assigned to the U.S. Naval Hospital at Cañacao, overlooking Manila Bay. A brief assignment to Guam during the typhoon of 1940 had tested her hand, but nothing quite prepared her for the war that arrived in December 1941.

When Japanese bombers struck American bases across Luzon after Pearl Harbor, Cobb and her ten fellow Navy nurses moved swiftly. They evacuated casualties to Sternberg Army Hospital in Manila and later improvised a treatment center on the grounds of St. Scholastica’s College, working alongside civilian and military doctors under German nuns.

When Manila was declared an open city and General Douglas MacArthur ordered the evacuation to Corregidor, the eleven Navy nurses stayed behind in the burning capital. They kept working. As fires raged across the city, Cobb and her team tended to the wounded until Japanese forces occupied Manila on January 2, 1942, placing the nurses under arrest and interring them at the University of Santo Tomas.

Faced with an occupying force unfamiliar with women in uniform, Cobb relied on her administrative composure to protect her staff, even directing the nurses to mislabel precious stocks of quinine as sodium bicarbonate to keep the anti-malarial drug out of enemy hands.

In March 1942, the nurses were moved into the main civilian internment camp at Santo Tomas. Inside the crowded compound, Cobb joined forces with Dr. Charles Leach of the Rockefeller Foundation to build a working hospital out of scarce supplies. When overcrowding and deteriorating conditions prompted the forced transfer of 800 civilian men to a new camp in Los Baños, Laguna, in May 1943, Cobb and her nurses volunteered to go with them. Carrying their official records hidden beneath her clothing, Cobb and her team established a 21-bed infirmary at Los Baños, brewing plant leaves for medicine and using rubber tree sap as adhesive while maintaining daily care under increasingly dire conditions.

Despite near-starvation diets and rampant illness, they administered the ward until American paratroopers and Filipino guerrillas broke through the gates on February 23, 1945, liberating the camp. *(The captured Army nurses, who arrived at Santo Tomas following the fall of Bataan and Corregidor in 1942, remained behind to manage the Manila camp when the Navy nurses left for Los Baños).*

After the war, Cobb was awarded the Bronze Star for her leadership. Though broader official recognition faltered in the post-war bureaucracy, their history endures. They had seen the full reach of the war: from Cañacao to Sternberg, St. Scholastica, Santo Tomas, and Los Baños. There was no letup, yet they came through it together—alive and unbroken. With Chief Cobb at the helm, the world came to know the Navy's Band of Eleven.
